questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to tell jokes that make everyone laugh
Why some people never laugh at jokes
How laughter works and why it's good for us
Why rats are more intelligent than we think
questions.why: Sam says they'll find out that laughter is good for you, and they hear how a laugh is produced.

questions.q: How does Neil react to Sam's joke about rats?
options: He laughs and says it's funny
He says he has heard it before
He doesn't understand it
He says it isn't funny at all

questions.q: What medical evidence about laughing does Neil mention?
options: It makes people sleep for longer at night
It stops people from catching Covid
It helps people lose weight quickly
People who laugh recover faster from illness
questions.why: Neil says laughing releases anti-stress endorphins and people who laugh recover more quickly from illness.

questions.q: What does Sam say about babies and laughter?
options: Babies laugh before they learn to cry
After crying, laughing is often their next sound
Babies don't laugh until they are about a year old
Babies only laugh when other people laugh first
questions.why: She says babies cry from birth, and the next sound they make, often at two or three months, is laughter.

questions.q: According to Professor Sophie Scott, how is a laugh produced?
options: By moving the tongue and lips very quickly
By breathing in air slowly through the nose
By the rib cage squeezing air out quickly
By using the voice in the same way as singing
questions.why: She says you get very large, fast contractions of the rib cage, squeezing air out in big bouts.

questions.q: Why does Sam mention words like 'chuckle', 'giggle' and 'guffaw'?
options: To show that English is hard to learn
To explain which laugh is the healthiest
To teach listeners some new jokes
To show laughter is shared by all humans
questions.why: She says crying and laughing link to a universal human experience, seen in the many words we use for them.

questions.q: According to Sophie Scott, what does laughter mean for young mammals?
options: It's an invitation to play
It's a sign that they are hungry
It's a warning to stay away
It's a way to call their mother
questions.why: She says laughter is 'a sort of an invitation to play, it's a sign that you're playing'.

questions.q: What happens to young rats that don't laugh back?
options: They are left alone by the other rats
They're more likely to get bitten
They are tickled until they laugh
They leave the group and live alone
questions.why: Neil says young rats who don't laugh back are more likely to get a bite than a giggle.
